title: BeeTracker
pitch: A general-purpose autolabeling pipeline that turns raw bee-hive footage into trajectory data using YOLO detection, ByteTrack tracking, and an iterative loop that trains its own detector.
tagline: Research in Zeynep Temel’s Zoom Lab at CMU: one researcher, raw hive video in, labeled trajectories out (in an afternoon instead of thousands of hand-drawn boxes).

sections.heading: Where this all began
body: This project began before I joined Zeynep Temel’s research team at CMU; it started at Cornell as Guadalupe Bernal’s Masters project, which produced hundreds of hours of bee-hive entrance footage. Hive-entrance video captures exactly what researchers need: foraging rate, traffic patterns, stress response. But raw footage is useless without labels, and training a reliable detector has usually meant hand-drawing thousands of bounding boxes per hive.

My job was to collapse that pipeline into software that tracks bee trajectories, tells when bees enter and exit the hive, and can train new YOLO models inside the app so anyone with a different camera setup can adapt it to their own footage.

sections.heading: Detection & tracking
body: Each frame passes through a fine-tuned YOLO detector. A ByteTrack layer links detections into persistent tracks, and a velocity-vector corrector recovers tracks missed between frames. Completed tracks are classified as entry, exit, or neither against a user-placed entrance zone, using a weighted score over displacement, velocity alignment, terminal proximity, and closest approach.

sections.heading: The autolabel loop
body: The core idea is an iterative loop that turns a text prompt into a fine-tuned bee detector: seed prompt, audit the data, train, generate labels, check performance, repeat. Each pass improves the next round of labels, and the detector picks up bee-specific cues as it goes.

sections.heading: Results
body: On a full session of hive footage the pipeline picks out the entries and exits and condenses the video into navigable motion segments. Tracks export to CSV or JSON, and a manual-override UI handles the edge cases. The whole capture rig is just a camera, a stand, and a mesh enclosure at an outdoor apiary.

The pipeline generalizes past bees. Anything that crosses a boundary is usable: ants at a nest, rats in a lab study, people walking through a doorway. You can load up any video, sketch an entrance, label a handful of frames, and the rest runs itself.
